properties.name: count
properties.description: total number of instances

properties.name: spacing
properties.description: distance along the path between instances in mm

properties.name: totalLength
properties.description: first-to-last distance along the path in mm instead of spacing

properties.name: start
properties.description: where the seed sits along the path, mm (default 0)

properties.name: startFraction
properties.description: where the seed sits as a fraction of the path length, 0 to 1

properties.name: flip
properties.description: run the path from its other end

properties.name: orientation
properties.description: 'fixed' (default) or 'tangent'

methods.summary: Surface: sew all surfaces so far into one body (a solid when they close).
methods.description: Knits every surface feature made earlier in the script. With solid: true a closed set becomes a solid body (knitNotClosed when there are gaps); with solid: false (default) the result stays a sheet.

properties.name: solid
properties.description: make a solid from a closed shell

methods.example:
part('Box from sheets')
  .sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(20, 20)).surfaceExtrude(10)
  .sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(20, 20)).surfacePlanar()
  .sketch(at('front', 10), (s) => s.rect(20, 20)).surfacePlanar()
  .knit({ solid: true });
methods.notes: - Sews all earlier surface features. solid: true needs a CLOSED set (a tube sheet plus its two planar caps): gaps give knitNotClosed. Check the end sketches are at the sheet ends (at('front', depth)).

methods.summary: Surface: extrude the last sketch into a sheet (no end caps, not a solid).
methods.description: Like extrude but the result is a surface body (open sheet). Use thicken() to give it a wall, or knit() a closed set of sheets into a solid. A closed profile gives a tube sheet open at both ends; an open sketch gives a ribbon.

properties.name: flip
properties.description: reverse direction

methods.summary: Surface: loft a sheet through section sketches (open or closed curves).
methods.description: Like loft() but the result is a surface body, so open curves (arcs, splines) work as sections. All sections should be the same kind (all open or all closed). The sheet is a surface body: thicken() works on planar and cylindrical sheets (a thicken of a doubly curved lofted sheet answers offsetUnsupported).

parameters.name: sections
parameters.description: list of { on, draw } section sketches, at least two

methods.summary: Surface: a flat sheet filling the last closed sketch.
methods.description: Makes a planar surface body from a closed profile. Use it to cap surface tubes before knit(solid: true).

methods.summary: Surface: give the last surface a wall thickness and make it a solid.
methods.description: Thickens the most recent surface feature (surfaceExtrude, surfacePlanar, surfaceLoft or knit) into a solid wall of this thickness. It fails on a surface that folds or has a pole (thickenFailed).

properties.name: op
properties.description: 'add' (default) or 'cut'

methods.notes:
- Needs a surface feature before it (surfaceExtrude, surfacePlanar, surfaceLoft, knit). Planar and cylindrical sheets work; a doubly curved lofted sheet answers offsetUnsupported and a sheet with a pole thickenPointedPole.
- A surface body has no volume: facts report area only until it is thickened or knitted into a solid.

methods.signature: .insertPart(doc: Record<string, unknown>, o: { at?: [number, number, number]; fixed?: boolean; name?: string } = {})
methods.summary: Assembly: insert another part (its document) as a component, optionally moved.
methods.description: Adds an insertPart feature that carries the whole part document (the .document of a runScript result, or a saved part). The component is its own body in the model, so a later mate() can position it. at moves it by [x, y, z] mm; fixed keeps mates from moving it. A part document is needed, not code: run the other script first. Assemblies live inside one part document; there is no separate assembly document in the script API.

parameters.name: o
parameters.type: { at?: [number, number, number]; fixed?: boolean; name?: string }

properties.name: at
properties.description: [x, y, z] placement in mm, default [0, 0, 0]

properties.name: fixed
properties.description: true to anchor the component

properties.name: name
properties.description: label for the component

methods.example:
const pin = { format: 'ck-part', version: 1, name: 'Pin', features: [], seq: 1, rollback: null };
part('Asm').insertPart(pin, { at: [10, 0, 0] });
methods.notes:
- Takes a part DOCUMENT (the .document of a finished run), not script text: run the component's script first. Assemblies live in the part document as insertPart + mate features.
- The n-th insertPart() call is component n in mate(): { part: n, face: 'F2.C1' } names face F2.C1 of the inserted part (suffix @F<insert id>.1 is added for you). fixed: true on the component that must not move.

A face is { part: n, face: 'F2.C1' }: the face named F2.C1 inside the n-th insertPart() call (1-based), or a persistent name string with the @component suffix, or face(sel) of the current body. flip reverses the alignment. The component that is not fixed moves, so insert the stationary one with fixed: true.

parameters.name: o
parameters.type: { kind: string; a: FaceSel | string | { part: number; face: string }; b: FaceSel | string | { part: number; face: string }; distance?: Num; angle?: Num; flip?: boolean }

properties.name: kind
properties.description: mate kind, e.g. 'coincident'

properties.description: first face: { part, face } | persistent name | face(sel)

methods.summary: A parameter written as an expression over the variables.
methods.description: expr('w/2') keeps the feature parameter linked to the variable w (stored as =w/2). Inside a sketch an expr contributes its current number only. Characters are limited to arithmetic and Math.*.
methods.example:
const { w } = variables({ w: 40 });
part('Bar').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(w, 10)).extrude(expr('w/4'));

methods.summary: Put the features recorded inside `build` in a named folder of the feature tree.
methods.description: The free-function form of part.group: group('Tach gauge', () => { ... }) applies to the part started last with part().
methods.example:
const p = part('Dash');
group('Panel', () => { p.sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(100, 50), 'Panel').extrude(5); });

methods.summary: Start a new part: the part the script builds; returns the fluent builder.
methods.description: Every script builds one part (the last wins); call part() to start a new part. Chain sketch, extrude, cut, holes, fillet, ... on the result. The name appears as the document name.

methods.summary: Colour, opacity and finish of the bodies a feature made (view only, no geometry change).
methods.description: appearance({ feature: handle, colour: '#1a1a1a', opacity: 0.18, finish: 'glass' }) styles the body (lump) the feature created; when the feature made several bodies (a pattern) all of them, and for a pattern the seed's own body too. feature is a handle from part.handle() or an id like 'F12' (body is the same). colour (or color) is '#rrggbb' or '#rgb'; opacity is 0.05 to 1 (below 1 the body is drawn as glass in the transparent pass; a click passes through a body below 0.35); finish is 'matte' | 'plastic' | 'chrome' | 'glass' | 'brushed'. { face: 'F3.C1' } or { face: 'F3.*' } (a persistent face name or prefix) or { face: handle } (all the faces a feature created) sets colour and finish of single faces; the opacity of a face is ignored. Stored in the document (appearance, faceAppearance), so the app, the snapshot renderer and a saved file show it. The part's own material is the default for bodies without an appearance.

parameters.name: o
parameters.description: { feature | body | face, colour?, opacity?, finish? }

methods.notes:
- Styling a PATTERN feature (linearPattern / circularPattern) styles the copies AND the seed's own body, because the seed body belongs to the seed feature. A look given to the seed explicitly wins field by field.
- A body is keyed by the feature that created it: a boss fused into an earlier body is part of that body (take the handle of the FIRST feature of the body), a feature made with newBody is its own body.
- finish 'brushed' and 'chrome' are metallic: they shift colours towards grey in renders (copper looks silver). Use 'plastic' or 'matte' for coloured parts.
- It changes view state only (no feature, no undo step); STEP export keeps no colours or body names, a .ckpart does.

methods.summary: Read the total surface area (mm2) of the part built so far.
methods.description: Like volume(): forces a build of what is recorded so far and a mass-properties query, cached until the next feature. Needs await.
methods.example:
const p = part('Cube').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(10, 10)).extrude(10);
const a = await p.area();   // 600

methods.signature: .expectBBox(box: { min?: Vec; max?: Vec; size?: Vec }, o: { tolerance?: number; tol?: number; body?: string } = {}): this
methods.summary: Check the bounding box of the part built so far.
methods.description: expectBBox({ min, max, size }, { tolerance }) checks the keys you give (each [x, y, z], world mm) to an ABSOLUTE tolerance in mm, default 1e-3 (tol is a short name). size checks the extents without caring where the part sits; { body: 'Name' } measures one body made with newBody. The box is the kernel's display box: the display mesh joined with the edge curves, never the control polygon of a spline or loft (a lofted body trimmed by a cylinder, the tapered disc, reads x and z within 60, y 0 to 18). It can fall short of a round or free-form face by the mesh's chord error: about 1e-3 on a radius-10 sphere, 5e-3 on a free-form extrusion, and up to 0.05 mm for a radius-5 cylinder inside a multi-body part (a per-body box comes from the mesh vertices and edge curves of that body's faces), so give the tolerance you can justify (0.05 for round bodies). No await needed. A failure is a run error: 'Line N: expected bbox max [60, 18, 60], got [60, 17.5, 60] (tolerance 0.001)'.

parameters.name: box
parameters.type: { min?: Vec; max?: Vec; size?: Vec }
parameters.description: { min?, max?, size? } each [x, y, z]

parameters.name: o
parameters.type: { tolerance?: number; tol?: number; body?: string }

properties.name: tolerance
properties.description: absolute tolerance in mm, default 1e-3 (alias tol)

properties.name: body
properties.description: check one named body instead of the whole part

methods.summary: Check the number of faces of the part built so far.
methods.description: expectFaceCount(n) fails with the actual count when it differs. A cheap regression check after patterns and fillets. No await needed.

methods.summary: Check that no face of the part is smaller than a given area (no slivers).
methods.description: expectMinFaceArea(a) fails and names the smallest face when it is smaller than a mm2 (the kernel's exact face areas; all faces of all bodies, or { body: 'Name' }). Use it after fillets, trims and booleans, which leave sliver faces when the numbers nearly coincide. Choose a from the part: 0.01 mm2 catches slivers of a machined part; a printed part may allow less. No await needed. A failure is a run error: 'Line N: expected every face to be at least 0.01 mm2, the smallest is face F12.S.l3 with 0.0004 mm2'.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: smallest allowed face area in mm2

properties.name: body
properties.description: check the faces of one named body instead of all faces

methods.summary: Check that the part built so far passes the kernel's validity check.
methods.description: expectValid() fails with the validator's first issue (code and entity) as an error with this line. No await needed.

methods.signature: .expectVolume(v: number, o: { tolerance?: number; tol?: number; abs?: number; body?: string } = {}): this
methods.summary: Check the volume of the part built so far; a mismatch is reported as an error with this line.
methods.description: expectVolume(v, { tolerance }) compares the kernel's exact volume (mm3, all bodies together) with v: |got - v| <= v * tolerance, a RELATIVE tolerance, default 1e-3 (0.1 %). { abs } gives an absolute tolerance in mm3 instead; { body: 'Name' } measures one body made with newBody (an unknown name is an error that lists the bodies). tol is a short name for tolerance. No await needed: it is a step, checked when the runner reaches it (a build of what is recorded so far, cached with other reads). A failure is listed in the run errors, as 'Line N: expected volume 48000, got 47961.37 (tolerance 1e-6 relative)', so the run reports an error; later checks still run and are listed too. Analytic references (boxes, cylinders) match to 1e-6; a lofted or swept body only to the tolerance you can justify (0.5 % is typical).

parameters.name: o
parameters.type: { tolerance?: number; tol?: number; abs?: number; body?: string }

properties.name: tolerance
properties.description: relative tolerance, default 1e-3 (alias tol)

properties.name: abs
properties.description: absolute tolerance in mm3 (instead of tolerance)

properties.name: body
properties.description: check one named body instead of all bodies

methods.notes: - tol is relative (default 1e-3); pass { abs } for mm3. A failed expectation is an error with its line; the run goes on, but an agent run with errors does not replace the document.

methods.summary: Read the number of faces of the part built so far.
methods.description: Counts the faces of the display body; cached until the next feature. Needs await.
methods.example:
const p = part('Block').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(40, 30)).extrude(20);
const n = await p.faceCount();   // 6

methods.summary: Read the faces of the part built so far: persistent name, kind, area, normal, centre, radius, feature.
methods.description: Returns a list of { name, kind ('plane' | 'cylinder' | 'sphere' | 'other'), area, normal (planar faces), center, radius (round faces), feature }. The name works in face('F3.C1'). Use it to find the face you mean before selecting it; the surface kind and radius are fitted from the display mesh. Forces a view build of what is recorded so far, cached until the next feature. Needs await.
methods.example:
const p = part('Plate').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(60, 40)).extrude(10).hole(face('>Z'), [0, 0], { diameter: 8 });
const bores = (await p.faces()).filter((f) => f.kind === 'cylinder');   // one R4 bore

methods.summary: Put the features recorded inside `build` in a named folder of the feature tree.
methods.description: group('Tach gauge', () => { ... }) tags every feature added by the calls inside (sketches, planes, solids, holes) with group: 'Tach gauge'; the tree shows consecutive features with the same group under one collapsible folder. Groups do not nest: an inner group replaces the outer one until it ends. Also available as the free function group(name, build).
methods.example:
const p = part('Dash');
p.group('Panel', () => { p.sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(100, 50), 'Panel').extrude(5); });

methods.summary: A handle on the feature recorded last, for face({ of }) and patterns.
methods.description: handle() returns an object naming the feature the previous call added (its id is filled in when the script runs): const boss = part.handle() after .extrude(15). Then face('>Z', { of: boss }) selects only the faces that feature created, faces({ createdBy: boss }) all of them, edges({ createdBy: boss }) their edges, and linearPattern(boss, ...) repeats it. After a sketch it names the sketch; after a hole() the hole feature (a hole's sketch is internal). Placing a handle costs nothing.
methods.notes: - Take the handle right AFTER the feature it names. A handle used before it is resolved gives a Line N error. The handle names a hole() feature, not the internal sketch of it.

methods.signature: .inertia(density: number = 1): Promise<{ mass: number; centreOfMass: Vec; firstMoment: Vec; tensor: number[][]; tensorOrigin: number[][]; principal: Vec; axes: Vec[] }>
methods.summary: Read the mass, first moments, inertia tensor and principal axes of the part built so far.
methods.description: Returns { mass (g), centreOfMass (mm), firstMoment (mass x centre about the origin, g mm), tensor (3x3 rows about the centre of mass, world axes, g mm2), tensorOrigin (the same about the origin), principal (the three principal moments, smallest first, g mm2), axes (the unit principal axes in the same order) }. Exact for the kernel's analytic faces. A hole removes mass and never changes the signs: the diagonal stays positive and the products of inertia are minus the integral of x*y. Forces a build and a mass-properties query, cached until the next feature. Needs await.
methods.returns: Promise<{ mass: number; centreOfMass: Vec; firstMoment: Vec; tensor: number[][]; tensorOrigin: number[][]; principal: Vec; axes: Vec[] }>
methods.example:
const p = part('Block').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(40, 30)).extrude(20);
const m = await p.inertia(7.85);   // steel: m.mass, m.tensor, m.principal, m.axes

methods.signature: .issues(): Promise<Array<{ code: string; entity: string; detail: string }>>
methods.summary: Read the validator's issues for the part built so far.
methods.description: Returns a list of { code, entity, detail }, empty when the part is valid. Needs await.
methods.returns: Promise<Array<{ code: string; entity: string; detail: string }>>
methods.example:
const p = part('Block').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(40, 30)).extrude(20);
const issues = await p.issues();   // []

methods.summary: Read whether the part built so far passes the kernel's validity check.
methods.description: true when the validator finds no issue; the issues come from part.issues(). Forces a build and a validate query, cached until the next feature. Needs await.
methods.example:
const p = part('Block').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(40, 30)).extrude(20);
const ok = await p.isValid();   // true

methods.signature: .textMetrics(string: string, opts: { font?: string; height?: Num; spacing?: Num } = {}): Promise<TextMetricsFact>
methods.summary: Measure a string before drawing it: width, ink box and per-letter advances.
methods.description: await part.textMetrics(string, { font, height, spacing }) asks the kernel for the real layout of the text (the same one s.text() uses) and returns { width, advance, bbox: [x0, y0, x1, y1], capHeight, chars, advances, warnings }; width is the ink width in mm, bbox is relative to the pen start on the baseline. Use it to size a nameplate, centre a label or fit a font height to a space. It needs await and costs one kernel request; no build is forced.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.type: { font?: string; height?: Num; spacing?: Num }
parameters.description: { font: 'gauge'|'engrave'|library id (default gauge), height: cap height mm (default 5), spacing: pitch factor (default 1) }

methods.notes:
- Needs await (one kernel request, no build). width is the INK width: size a plate as m.width + 2 x margin and centre the text with anchor ['center', 'middle'].
- Same layout as s.text(): pass the same font, height and spacing.

methods.summary: Z-up or Y-up view hint.
methods.description: 'z' for a model built along Z (a bottle, a motor). Stored in the document as the field upAxis, not geometry: the app opens with the camera Z-up (or Y-up) so the model stands upright. The kernel ignores it; View > Up axis still switches.

methods.summary: Read the volume (mm3) of the part built so far.
methods.description: await part.volume() makes the runner build everything recorded up to here on the scratch kernel (a full regeneration of the features so far, then a mass-properties query), returns the number and the script continues recording. Use it to compute the next dimension from a real result or to print a check. The script must use await (top level await is allowed). COST: every read forces an intermediate build; the answer is cached until the next feature is added, so read once, after a group of features, not inside a loop of features. Compare with the expect* helpers, which need no await.
methods.notes:
- Needs `await`. Every read forces an intermediate regeneration of everything recorded so far (a full build on the scratch kernel, a view build for bbox/faces/counts); the answer is cached until the next feature is added. Read once after a group of features, never inside a loop that adds features.
- Use the expect* helpers (expectVolume, expectValid, expectBBox, expectFaceCount) when you only want to assert: no await, errors carry the script line.

methods.signature: variables(defs: Record<string, number | string>): Record<string, number>
methods.summary: Declare named values; strings are expressions over earlier ones.
methods.description: variables({ w: 60, t: 'w/10' }) defines document variables (editable in the Variables tab) and returns their numbers for use in the script. Use expr('w*2') to keep a feature parameter linked to a variable instead of a fixed number.
methods.example:
const { w, t } = variables({ w: 60, t: 'w/10' });
part('Bar').sketch('front', (s) => s.rect(w, 10)).extrude(expr('t'));
